text.p: Australia announced an unexpected fall in employment on Thursday, sending the local dollar sharply lower and debt futures higher.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics said the total number of people employed dropped by 40,300 in May, pushing the unemployment rate to 8.8 percent. Forecasts had centred on a 15,000 employment rise with unemployment staying at 8.7 percent.
Economists said the data increased chances for another interest rate cut to jump-start the economy although they pointed out that employment was a "lagging indicator" which reflected past weakness.
"This is just unambiguously scary," said Annette Beacher, senior economist with Citibank Australia. "It is just very, very bad economic news here."

Added Susan Creighton, chief economist at ABM-Amro: "It certainly increases the prospects of another interest rate cut in the near term because I think everybody's going to be very worried about the employment situation ..."
The Australian dollar, which was badly hit by the last rate cut on May 23, was quoted at US$0.7509/14 around midday shortly after the jobs data release, down from an earlier US$0.7563/68.
June 10-year bond futures were at 92.900 against a pre-data 92.775. September bill futures also rose.
Official interest rates have been cut four times in the past year, partly in an attempt to boost spending and combat high unemployment, which has been stuck above 8.5 percent for the past year.
But consumer confidence is still sluggish even though home loan rates are at their lowest in more than 20 years.
Employment Minister Amanda Vanstone said the May labour force figures were consistent with the view that employment growth would not come about until later in 1997.
"The flat state of the labour market is consistent with the widely held view that substantial employment growth will not occur until later this year," Vanstone said in a statement.
She said this was supported by economic forecasts and leading indicators of employment.
Australia's seasonally-adjusted estimate of the number of employed persons fell 40,300 in May to 8.380 million.
The seasonally-adjusted unemployment rate rose to 8.8 percent from 8.7 percent, compared with 8.5 percent a year earlier.

Vanstone said last week's economic growth figures for the March quarter augured well for employment growth in coming months. Australia's gross domestic product grew 0.9 percent in the March quarter from the previous quarter to stand 2.4 percent above its level a year earlier.
"It was undeniably a weak number," Bruce Hockman, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said of the jobs data.

"Obviously it was weaker than people were looking for and if you look at the way the markets are reacting then it is seen as something of a signal that there is more scope to ease policy. Perhaps they are seeing that it is more urgent to ease policy."
